title: Free build week three: the real test
summary: Finish your build, put it in the hands of the person it is for, adopt one improvement from what their hands teach you, and draft the science fair board from your log.
materials: your free build, nearly finished, and its parts
your plan, change list and budget sheet from weeks 9 and 10
pencil, markers and loose printed photos or drawings for the board
the person the build is for, or a stand-in, for a ten minute test

steps.title: Finish is a decision
steps.body:
The design loop, one last time for this build: ask, imagine, plan, build, test, fix. Weeks 9 and 10 spent the first four. This week belongs to test and fix, and to the strange discovery every builder makes: finished is not something that happens to a build. It is something you decide about a build.

Decide it with three questions. Does it do the one job it was built to do, the job you said in one sentence back in week 9? Is it safe and solid enough to hand over without you delivering a warning speech first? Could the person use it without you standing next to it explaining? Three yeses is finished. Anything still missing after three yeses is decoration, and decoration must never hold the build hostage.

If week 10's wall is still standing, it gets the first fifteen minutes today, with fresh eyes and the bug diary open to the exact question you wrote as its last line. A precise question after a night of sleep is how most walls actually fall.

One more clock to read: the reveal is next week. Week 9 taught you that a budget cap decides what gets bought. Time is a cap too, and this week it decides what gets built. Spend your minutes on the three yeses first, exactly the way you spent your dollars on the core parts first.

Five minutes on your typing site, eyes on the screen. Today's words are the board's words: type Question, Plan, Trials, Result five times each, because your hands will letter them large on the tri-fold later. Then type your build's own question, the one sentence naming the person and the problem, twice without looking down. Finish with this week's verbs: finished, tested, improved, delivered.

steps.title: Finish it
steps.body:
Write the short list: everything standing between the build as it sits and the three yeses. Sort it into must and nice. Musts get built now; nices go to the next time list without guilt.

Work the musts the week 10 way: one piece at a time, retest the core after each piece. A build can be broken by its last screw as easily as by its first, and the only way to know is to check. Any surprise goes into the bug diary in the usual four lines: expected, happened, tried, then what happened next.

When the third yes arrives, stop building and say it out loud: this build is finished. Then, and only then, spend leftover minutes on decoration.

Close the money story too: the change list from week 10 gets its final prices, and the budget sheet gets its final total, sitting next to the cap. The pay yourself first money is still not part of this. That number is the last line of the build's money story, and the board will want it.
checklist: The short list is written and split into must and nice
Every must is done, and the core was retested after each piece went on
I said the three yeses out loud: it does the job, it is safe to hand over, it works without me
The budget sheet shows the final total next to the cap, with the pay yourself first money untouched
Everything unfinished lives on the next time list, not inside the build

items.s: Blind test vs the builder's own eyes
Blind test: expecting brain taken out of the loop
The builder is the worst tester: expectations steer

steps.title: Why builders are the worst testers
steps.body:
Here is a strange fact from real laboratories: scientists testing a new medicine do not let the doctors know which patients got the real pill. Why? Because expecting something changes what you see. A doctor who hopes the medicine works will honestly, without lying, see patients as a little healthier. The brain quietly bends what it notices toward what it expects. Scientists call it bias, and their fix is ruthless: blind the test, take the expecting brain out of the loop.

Now look at your bench. You are the worst possible tester for your own build, and not because you are careless. The opposite: you know it too well. You hold it the gentle way without noticing, press the good button, avoid the wobbly corner by habit. Your expectations steer your hands around every weakness. A stranger's hands have no such map. They will grab it wrong, press hard, try the thing you never imagined, and find in one minute what you could not find in a week.

That is not a threat. It is the entire treasure of the next step. When the person stumbles, your build is not failing a test; your build is finally getting a real one. Test it or trust it, from week 1, has one more verse: a build tested only by its own builder is still a take-my-word-for-it claim.

steps.title: The real test
steps.body:
Hand the build to the person it is for. If it is still a secret gift, recruit a stand-in who matches them as closely as you can, someone with similar hands and habits, and save the true handover for next week's reveal. If the person lives far away, a video call test works: they watch nothing; you follow their instructions with their eyes on the build.

Say one sentence only: this is for you to try, show me how you would use it. Then sit on your hands and let their hands do the talking.

Your job is the tally. A stumble is any moment they pause, ask a question, hold it wrong, or use it differently than your plan imagined. Mark each stumble and jot what caused it. Week 10's interview habits apply exactly: wait out silences, never defend, never rescue. If your fingers itch to grab the build and show them the right way, that itch is data, because at the science fair and after the gift is given, you will not be there to grab it.

Catch two more things in their exact words: what they said at the moment they liked it most, and what they said at the moment that annoyed or confused them most. Both sentences belong on the board. Then thank them, like an engineer thanking a test pilot.
checklist: I said one sentence and then let their hands do the talking
Every stumble is tallied, each with a note of what caused it
Their exact words at the best moment and the worst moment are written down
I did not explain, defend or rescue the build, not even once

steps.title: Testing it on the real person
steps.body:
What the person is asked to do with the build stays the same for every trial. Only the trial number changes, and nothing about the build is adjusted between trials.

Watch the real person use the build at least three times. For each trial, write the trial number and how many seconds it took them to use it, timed the same way each time.
steps.question: How much did the person's time change from their first trial to their last, and did it get faster or slower?

steps.title: Improve it once
steps.body:
Read the stumble tally like data, because it is data. Which single change would erase the biggest stumble? That change, and only that change, goes into the build today.

Say the pick out loud in one line before touching anything: I am changing this so that that stops happening. If you cannot fill in both halves of the sentence, you have a decoration in mind, not an improvement, so pick again.

Make the change the disciplined way: one thing at a time, core retested after, bug diary open in case the fix breaks something its own way. Fixes are changes, and changes are exactly how bugs arrive.

Every other idea from the test goes on the next time list. Do not mourn them. A science fair board that says here is what I would do next is stronger than one pretending the build is perfect, and next week's talk will say it proudly.
checklist: One improvement chosen, and my one line names the stumble it erases
The change went in alone, one thing at a time, and the core was retested after
The bug diary got a line for anything the change surprised me with
The remaining ideas are on the next time list, not squeezed into the build

figure.alt: A tri-fold board outline divided into four labelled areas: Question across the top naming the person and the problem in one sentence, Plan on the left with the sketch, priced list and pay-yourself-first line, Trials on the right with the first working photo, a wall and its fix, the stumble tally and the one improvement, and Result across the bottom with what the build does now, the final total against the cap, and the next time list. A note says headlines must read from three steps away and at least one wall must stay on the board.

items.s: RESULT: what it does now, total vs cap, next time list
Headlines readable from three steps away;
keep at least one wall on the board

steps.title: Draft the board
steps.body:
Lay the tri-fold flat and give each beat of the story its place. Center top: Question, the person and the problem in one sentence. Left panel: Plan, your week 9 sketch and the priced list, with the pay yourself first line visible. Right panel: Trials, the honest middle of the story: the first working photo from week 10, your best wall from the bug diary and how it fell, the stumble tally from today, and the one improvement with its one line. Center bottom: Result, what the build does now, the final total against the cap, and the next time list as what I would do next.

Everything comes from pages you already have. The Maker's Log, the bug diary, the change list and the budget sheet wrote this board across three weeks; today you are only arranging it.

Two rules of the board trade. Headlines big: a stranger three steps away should catch the whole story from the four beat words alone. And truth on the board: at least one thing that went wrong stays on it. Judges have seen a hundred perfect boards; they remember the honest one.

Glue nothing. Lay the pieces and pencil the headings, because tomorrow's rehearsal with the skeptical judge will move something, and a board that can still move is a board that can still improve.
checklist: All four beats have a home: question, plan, trials, result
The board tells the truth: at least one wall and its fix is on it, not only wins
The headings read from three steps away
Nothing is glued; every piece can still move after the rehearsal

steps.title: Show it
steps.prompt: Photo of the finished build after its one improvement, a photo of the test notes with the stumble tally, and a photo of the whole board draft laid out. If your build is a program, add the final code or a share link too.
